5.0.s.en: (1) The fruits of the righteousness of Christ

5.0.0.en: When we received justification by faith, which is the forgiveness of sins in Baptism and the beginning of a life of holiness by the Holy Spirit in the anointing of the Myron, we came to be at peace with God, and this reconciliation was accomplished through our Lord Jesus Christ. The faith here is the faith of the one baptized if he is an adult, or the faith of his parents if he is a child.

5.1.0.en: Through Christ also "we have access." The word "have" means that we were changed from the position of the sinner, rejected and driven away, to the justified, beloved one, called to enter the fold of Christ by faith, to enjoy the grace of redemption, then justification, then peace.

5.1.1.en: The phrase (we stand) means continuing to enjoy grace, and this is by means of the sacrament of repentance and confession, which is a renewal of Baptism.

5.1.2.en: And we also boast and rejoice in what we await of the glory that God prepares for us in heaven.

5.2.0.en: Tribulations, instead of being a source of the Christian's feeling of oppression and injustice, have become a source of pride and glory for him. Why? Because tribulations train us in patience and endurance.

5.3.0.en: The patient one is proved, that is, succeeds in the test of faith, since he did not doubt God during the trial, and the one who succeeds has hope that he will inherit eternal life, and everyone who has put his hope in Christ will not be disappointed. What makes us endure tribulations is that the Holy Spirit, poured out in our hearts, constantly assures us of God's love for us, so we fear no evil.

5.3.1.en: Do not look, beloved, at the bitterness of the tribulation, but at the tender hand of God that controls the tribulation, for nothing will befall you from it except what is for your good on earth and for your glory in heaven.

5.4.s.en: (2) Christ the Righteous, Redeemer of sinners

5.4.0.en: We came to know God's love for us even more when Christ died for us, since because of our weakness we persisted in sin.

5.5.0.en: Righteous: pure, with his sins forgiven. Good: pure and doing good works.

5.5.1.en: Human logic teaches us that scarcely will a person die for a righteous man occupied with worship and piety, or perhaps a person will die for a good man (who is more excellent than the righteous man in his service, his good works, and his giving of himself for others). But who is it that dies and sacrifices his life for an ungodly man, who does not deserve life at all?!!

5.6.0.en: Here Christ shows the greatness of His love for mankind, when He, the Righteous, died for sinners like me and you.

5.7.0.en: Just as Christ began our salvation with power when we were sinners, all the more will He complete our salvation on the heavenly level, so that we are spared punishment on the day of wrath (judgment), on condition that we walk in a life of righteousness and piety.

5.8.0.en: Here St. Paul brings us to a logical idea, which is that since Christ, when He was dead in the flesh, was the cause of our reconciliation, we sinners, with the Father, then all the more, after we have received reconciliation, we receive salvation by growing in His love and cleaving to Him.

5.8.1.en: We shall be saved by His life: St. Paul reveals an important part of the work of salvation, which is the life of the Lord Christ Himself, and it includes:

5.8.2.en: His life in the flesh, which He lived on earth, in which He fulfilled all righteousness on our behalf, so that He became pleasing to the Father on behalf of our humanity, and became an example for us to follow.

5.8.3.en: His life in our body: when we partake of His most holy Body and Blood, He abides in us and we in Him. Then He works in us and through us good works pleasing to the Father, which become a cause of our salvation.

5.9.0.en: Thus we rejoice and boast in our reconciliation with God, who ordered the moment of the salvation of mankind through His Son, whom He gave for us. And here St. Paul draws our attention to the fact that salvation is not the work of the Son only, but is also by the ordering of the Father, that we may rejoice and boast in the Father and the Son.

5.9.1.en: If you, my brother, have been reconciled with God, make use of His love by establishing a strong relationship with Him, being careful about your prayers, your meditations in His word, and going to His house (the Church), to strengthen your relationship with Him and even to experience new depths of His love. And let you have a renewed aspiration every day toward God.

5.10.s.en: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

5.10.0.en: When Adam sinned by eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and despised God's clear warning, "in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die," he brought sin into the world for the first time, for it had been unknown before, and consequently he received the penalty of death. Adam bequeathed to his offspring the corrupt nature, which knows evil and is weak in resisting it, and death, as the wages of sin, passed upon all men. In another translation, the Jesuit translation from the Greek text, it says "in whom all have sinned" instead of "for that all have sinned," that is, all mankind were in the loins of Adam when he sinned, so they sinned in him, like a slave who married a bondwoman and they bore slaves.

5.11.0.en: Is not imputed: its guilt is not shown and defined except by the Law, because man had warped the natural law within him, which is the conscience, by his distance from God. So he was no longer able to distinguish wrong from right.

5.11.1.en: Of course sin existed in the world from Adam until the coming of the Law, as proved by the existence of the wicked such as Cain and the people of Sodom... and so on. The wicked thought that God would not count their sins against them, because He had not yet sent down the Law (the statute) by which He would judge them. So they walked by the law of the jungle and deserved death, although they should have walked by the voice of God within them, which is the conscience.

5.12.0.en: After the similitude of Adam's transgression: the same sin as Adam's, though their sins were less.

5.12.1.en: The righteous also died, who did not sin like Adam, the transgressor against God. And perhaps you, reader, ask: what then is the fault of the righteous like Noah and Abraham, who pleased God and whose sins were few and limited?

5.12.2.en: Here St. Paul reassures us that the justice and mercy of God will set things right with the coming of the One to come (Christ), who is like Adam in His effectiveness and influence upon all mankind. The first Adam bequeathed to us death through sin, and Christ bequeathed to us life through righteousness.

5.12.3.en: In verses (15-19) St. Paul will draw a comparison between the sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ, the sum of which is that the blessings Christ (the second Adam) brought us exceed by thousands of times the death through sin which Adam "the first man" brought us.

5.13.0.en: If the sin of Adam has spread through the whole human race, the grace of Christ justifies those who believe in Him and fills their lives with holiness. That is, the grace of Christ is overflowing and sufficient for everyone who believes in Him.

5.14.0.en: If Adam bequeathed his sin to mankind, the grace of Christ forgives not only the ancestral sin but all the sins that people have committed, and they receive a new, pure nature in Baptism, and indeed their sins are forgiven many times afterward in the sacrament of repentance and confession.

5.15.0.en: Death reigned: all died because of the sin of Adam.

5.15.1.en: Shall reign by One: they receive the Kingdom through Christ.

5.15.2.en: The sin of Adam brought death upon all mankind, while the grace of Christ gives believers to reign forever with Christ in the heavens.

5.16.0.en: Just as the sin of Adam spread in the human race, so the righteousness of Christ frees them from the final judgment and gives them eternal happiness.

5.17.0.en: All inherited sin through the sin of Adam, while the obedience of Christ gives purity and new life to all believers.

5.17.1.en: Do not submit to sin, for it is an intruder upon us. Let us repent and enjoy the righteousness of Christ, and continue our striving in a spiritual walk until we reign forever in the heavens.

5.18.0.en: By this it appears that Christ has the whole role in justification, and the Law has no role.

5.18.1.en: Why then did the Law come?

5.18.2.en: It came "that the offence might abound," that is, become clear, and to nullify the argument of mankind that sin is not imputed when there is no law (ch. 5:13). The Law came carrying a long list of prohibitions without any loopholes, to close to mankind the opportunity of falling into sins on the pretext that they did not know they were sins. So the Law was like a mirror that revealed to mankind the hideousness and multitude of its sins. But just as the names, forms, and kinds of sins multiplied through the Law, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ multiplied and surpassed and overflowed, so that it can forgive and blot out every iniquity however great.

5.18.3.en: If you live in difficult circumstances that try to keep you away from God, do not be troubled. Flee from them as much as you can, and be confident that the power of God supports you and keeps you with greater help than the one who lives in ordinary circumstances. That is, do not blame circumstances when you sin, but repent and ask God's help, and you will overcome sin however difficult or dominating it may be.

5.19.0.en: The conclusion is: if you, O man, are grieved because the sin of Adam brought us death of the body after the misery of life, although we are not directly responsible for Adam's eating from the tree, behold, Christ died for us without guilt so that we might inherit eternal life, if we walk in a life of righteousness by faith and works, relying on the grace of Christ.

5.19.1.en: Baptism and striving to obtain justification

6.0.s.en: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

6.0.0.en: St. Paul condemns the opinion of the sinners who say that if God increases His grace and mercy toward those who have fallen into severe sins and difficult circumstances in order to help them come out of them, then let us remain in a life of sin to receive God's many mercies.

6.1.1.en: St. Paul denies this opinion, because if God in His abundant mercy poured out upon us His rich graces to remove from us every trace of sin, this does not push us to carelessness and persisting in sin. Then he explains that by Baptism we have become like a dead being in relation to sin, so that when it attacks us it finds in us no senses to be seduced and no members to carry out sin.

6.2.0.en: Were baptized into Jesus Christ: received Christian Baptism, in faith in Christ the Savior. Were baptized into His death: the more exact translation is "was baptized in His death," that is, he dies with Christ when he goes down into the water of Baptism and rises with Him.

6.2.1.en: The value of Baptism is very great, because in it we die with Christ to our sins. By His death He took away our sins and saved us from them.

6.3.0.en: By Baptism we share with Christ in His death and His resurrection, which was accomplished by the glory of the Father (by the power of the Father), so we are buried that the old man, weak before sin, may die in us, and then we rise as a man born anew, walking in newness of life with a holy conduct. So life by Baptism is like the process of creation.

6.4.0.en: The likeness of His death: immersion in the water of Baptism, which resembles the death of Christ on the Cross.

6.4.1.en: We shall be also in the likeness of His resurrection: we live the life of resurrection and victory over sin and enjoy fellowship with Christ. When we were baptized and sin died in us in a form like the death of Christ on the Cross, we were united with Him in a close union, so our self became one with His, and we enjoyed the joy of the resurrection with Him. That is the first resurrection in our life, when sin dies in us and we live to righteousness, as the Lord Christ said about the prodigal son: "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found" (Lk 15:24).

6.5.0.en: The old man: the old corrupt nature inherited from Adam, inclined to evil. The old man died with Christ in a mysterious way when He was crucified on the Cross. And by the death of the old man, "the body of sin" was destroyed, that is, sin became no longer in force over us, because we died in relation to it.

6.5.1.en: This reminds us of the saying of St. Augustine, when a woman came to him after his repentance, who had been accustomed to practice sin with him in a past time, and he said to her, "The Augustine whom you knew is dead." By this man is freed from the dominion of sin over him, and does not become its slave.

6.6.0.en: Also he is freed, that is, there is no longer anything that binds him to sin, and it no longer has dominion over him, and its relationship with him has ended.

6.7.0.en: Just as we shared with Christ in death when we were buried in the water of Baptism, so we rise with Him with a new holy nature that does not incline to evil, as He rose with a body of light.

6.8.0.en: What makes us confident of our spiritual resurrection in Baptism is that we believed there is a resurrection, because Christ has risen from the dead and will never die again, since He is a holy, living God who does not die, but died by His own will for our sins, and then rose to live in oneness with the Father. Thus everyone who is baptized dies to sin and lives in righteousness to please God.

6.8.1.en: The phrase once points to the fact that Baptism is not repeated, just as Christ also died once.

6.8.2.en: Remember at the beginning of every day your new nature which you received in Baptism, that you may live a new life for Christ, seeing Him before you in every work and word to please Him and to offer love to everyone you meet.

6.9.0.en: After St. Paul drew our attention to the divine factor in the process of salvation and justification, he moves to the human factor, advising you, after you have become clean, wearing the garments of salvation, not to return again to being soiled in the mud of sin, but let your members become living members to carry out God's will in you.

6.9.1.en: You who have been freed from the slavery of sin, do not return to sell yourself cheaply to it and become its slave again, obeying its commands over your body, which has gone back to desiring the pleasure of sin. And why, after Christ put to death in you, in Baptism, the various passions, do you return to bring them to life again, stirring and activating them with your senses when you expose them to external influences and stimuli, so that you descend once more to the bottom of sin?

6.10.0.en: Baptism frees you from the dominion of sin but does not give you immunity from error. If your body is dead to sin, why do you stir it with passions until sin reigns over it a second time?

6.11.0.en: Do not make your members doers of sin. Do not make your tongue abusive, nor your hand striking, nor your body fornicating as though it were an animal body stripped of reason and wisdom; rather, offer yourself, which is your soul, your thought, your mind, and your heart, as a living person aware of the value of your soul and as a son of God who does righteousness with all the members he has been given (praying / serving)...

6.12.0.en: In this way sin will not be able to lord it over you, because you are not in the age of the Law, which was limited to rebuking man for his sins without giving him any power to overcome, but you are now in the age of grace, the grace of the Holy Spirit who works in you with a mysterious power, and the love of Christ that surrounds you, and the care of the Father who helps you. And in this your members are strengthened, and you overcome and triumph.

6.13.s.en: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

6.13.0.en: Strangely, some in the age of grace misused their understanding of the freedom that is in Christ, and turned to license. Here St. Paul strongly condemns the baptized, purified person walking in evil.

6.14.0.en: Man, as the Lord Christ said, "No man can serve two masters" (Mt 6:24), is either an obedient slave to sin in its commands over his body, and the result will be spiritual death for him and man becomes like an animal body; or he is obedient to God's commandments, and so becomes righteous.

6.14.1.en: Beware, beloved... for your obedience to sin is obedience to the devil himself, who gives deceptive names to sin to lessen its impact on a person's conscience lest he repent, such as calling fornication the sins of youth, anger strength of personality, and greed ambition... and so on.

6.15.0.en: Which you received from the apostles: here St. Paul points to the importance of the apostolic tradition as a source of teaching alongside the Gospel.

6.15.1.en: You obeyed from the heart: this makes clear that Christianity is not outward moral commandments but love from the heart, which leads to obeying His commandments and walking in the commandment.

6.15.2.en: The form of doctrine: this affirms that the teaching depended on an example seen in the lives of the teachers, and not merely words or theoretical preaching.

6.15.3.en: Here St. Paul thanks God, not because they lived as slaves of sin, but because they left that way and followed with all their hearts the teachings of Christ which they received from the apostles.

6.16.0.en: When you were freed from sin, you became servants, by your own free will, of God, carrying out His commandments.

6.17.0.en: I speak after the manner of men: that is, in an easy, simple human style, so that souls weak toward sin may understand it.

6.17.1.en: Unto iniquity: out of love for it.

6.17.2.en: Since you readily accepted slavery to sin, and your members were doing uncleanness and iniquity out of love for it, the time has now come for the members to become holy, working righteousness, so that you become saints.

6.18.1.en: a- The way of evil and passions; whoever walks in it becomes a slave of the devil, free from the commandments of Christ.

6.18.2.en: b- The spiritual way; whoever walks in it is a servant of his Master Jesus Christ, the King of Peace, freed from any dominion of sin over him.

6.18.3.en: Satan comes, beloved, deceiving and saying: Come, be free from all the restraints of the commandment. Why do you weary your body with fasting? Why do you deprive your body of pleasure, enjoyment, and sin? Why do you guard your tongue from error?

6.18.4.en: So come, do what is pleasing in your eyes, free from the commandments of the Gospel that lead to righteousness. But you, beloved, as soon as you obtain this false, so-called freedom, find yourself leaving the righteousness of the compassionate God who loves mankind, who gives peace on earth and eternity in heaven, and entering under the dominion of cruel Satan who hates mankind, so he humiliates and shatters your life and your future and even your eternity.

6.19.0.en: Then St. Paul returns, posing a question: what fruit did you have as a result of this former life, in which you did evils of which you are now ashamed? And because you repented of them, you were delivered from eternal death, that is, the punishment of Gehenna.

6.20.0.en: But now, after you have been freed from sin and have become beloved servants of God, you have received the fruits of the Holy Spirit, "love, joy, peace... and so on," and then God will reward you in the end with eternal life.

6.21.0.en: Then St. Paul comes to the sum of life: if you commit sins and do not repent of them, you will die an eternal death. But to the one who walks in righteousness God gives eternal life, which our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ opened before us.

6.21.1.en: Christ frees me from the Law and saves me from sin
